original_value: Extreme rainfall has caused severe road damage and landslide disasters in mountainous areas. Rainfall forecasting derived from remote sensing data has been widely adopted for disaster prevention and early warning as a trend in recent years. By integrating high-resolution radar rain data, for example, the QPESUMS (quantitative precipitation estimation and segregation using multiple sensors) system provides a great opportunity to establish the extreme climate-based landslide susceptibility model, which would be helpful in the prevention of hillslope disasters under climate change. QPESUMS was adopted to obtain spatio-temporal rainfall patterns, and further, multi-temporal landslide inventories (2003–2018) would integrate with other explanatory factors and therefore, we can establish the logistic regression method for prediction of landslide susceptibility sites in the Laonong River watershed, which was devastated by Typhoon Morakot in 2009. Simulations of landslide susceptibility under the critical rainfall (300, 600, and 900 mm) were designed to verify the model’s sensitivity. Due to the orographic effect, rainfall was concentrated at the low mountainous and middle elevation areas in the southern Laonong River watershed. Landslide change analysis indicates that the landslide ratio increased from 1.5% to 7.0% after Typhoon Morakot in 2009. Subsequently, the landslide ratio fluctuated between 3.5% and 4.5% after 2012, which indicates that the recovery of landslide areas is still in progress. The validation results showed that the calibrated model of 2005 is preferred in the general period, with an accuracy of 78%. For extreme rainfall typhoons, the calibrated model of 2009 would perform better (72%). This study presented that the integration of multi-temporal landslide inventories in a logistic regression model is capable of predicting rainfall-triggered landslide risk under climate change.

result.paraphrase: Intense rainfall has led to serious road destruction and landslide disasters in mountainous regions. In recent years, rainfall forecasting based on remote sensing data has been widely used as a disaster prevention and early-warning trend. By combining high-resolution radar rainfall data, the QPESUMS (quantitative precipitation estimation and segregation using multiple sensors) system offers a strong basis for building an extreme climate-based landslide susceptibility model, which can aid in preventing hillslope disasters under climate change. QPESUMS was used to derive spatio-temporal rainfall patterns, and multi-temporal landslide inventories (2003–2018) were integrated with other explanatory factors to establish a logistic regression method for predicting landslide susceptibility sites in the Laonong River watershed, which was devastated by Typhoon Morakot in 2009. Landslide susceptibility simulations under critical rainfall levels of 300, 600, and 900 mm were designed to test the model’s sensitivity. Owing to the orographic effect, rainfall was concentrated in the low mountainous and middle elevation areas of the southern Laonong River watershed. Landslide change analysis shows that the landslide ratio rose from 1.5% to 7.0% after Typhoon Morakot in 2009. After 2012, the landslide ratio then fluctuated between 3.5% and 4.5%, indicating that recovery of landslide areas is still underway. Validation results indicated that the calibrated 2005 model is preferable for the general period, with 78% accuracy. For extreme-rainfall typhoons, the calibrated 2009 model performs better, at 72%. This study demonstrates that integrating multi-temporal landslide inventories into a logistic regression model can predict rainfall-triggered landslide risk under climate change.
